answers.Q1: Without the default refusal, running one selected test could overwrite the full generated spec with only that test’s scenario. Users would silently lose the rest of the suite’s scenarios and their real recorded outcomes, leaving an incomplete and misleading spec. The project treats the spec as a whole-suite artifact, so partial updates require the explicit `--specdeck-merge` choice.
answers.Q2: `depends_on` describes relationships for humans, blocking explanations, and reports; it is not a scheduler. Specdeck preserves pytest’s normal collection/execution order so it does not introduce hidden ordering or change test semantics. A dependency blocks only when its failed prerequisite actually ran earlier; a later prerequisite cannot retroactively prevent a test from running.
answers.Q3: A near-complete scenario list is noise rather than useful routing information: it makes the agent context large, scales badly, and can falsely suggest that every listed scenario specifically checks the function. Those scenarios merely execute a shared hub such as setup or configuration code. Reporting `most (N of M)` honestly conveys broad use while warning that execution is not proof or a useful shortlist of affected tests.
answers.Q4: The project guarantees that every `depends_on` reference in a generated spec resolves to an actual generated scenario, even when parametrized-case IDs collide with other scenario IDs and are deduplicated.
answers.Q5: It protects a CI report that gives users correct actionable statuses: outcomes come from the spec’s status tags, and skipped dependents are shown as blocked by the underlying failure, including multi-level cascades regardless of document order, rather than being misleadingly reported as ordinary skips or not run.
answers.Q9: They are opt-in so adopting specdeck is observational by default: it generates documentation and reports without unexpectedly breaking an existing suite or CI because requirements, covers links, or generated-spec validation are incomplete. Teams turn gates on only when they deliberately want those policies to enforce a release or quality boundary.
answers.Q10: It protects the documented meaning of dependencies: only an earlier failed prerequisite blocks a scenario, while a later one does not block it at all. The project cares because agents and developers use this document to interpret failures, coverage references, and the board; an incorrect scheduling mental model would lead them to misdiagnose blocked work or assume specdeck reorders tests when it deliberately does not.

commands: rg -n "gate|partial|depends_on|most \(" README.md docs specdeck tests | head -200
